bd99ac24a948d15e: AI has become a juggernaut, driving technical strategy in the tech sector and outside of it. With the worldwide server market growing 30 percent in a single year to hit $122.6bn in the first quarter of 2025, IDC now feels safe recategorizing AI-driven investment "from cyclical to durable".
The analyst company expects inference to account for over 70 percent of computing demand by next year, adding that it's growing fastest at the edge.
Why enterprises are building their own

All this investment in AI infrastructure might once have come mainly for hyperscalers, but that's changing quickly. Adoption is spreading quickly beyond public cloud service providers into enterprise environments, IDC adds. They're eager to run agentic AI in-house.

There are plenty of reasons for companies to own their own AI infrastructure rather than offloading it to the cloud. One of these is data control, especially in regulated sectors such as finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and the public sector that have sovereign data requirements. Another revolves around the need for predictable costing from tokens delivered on tunable in-house systems.

So what should companies look for in a supplier? Delivery speed will be a powerful driver for many who are under the gun to deliver AI initiatives for the business, especially during periods of constrained memory and CPU supply. Life cycle services will also come near the top of the list, for companies that need help managing everything from the power through to the reasoning LLM models and the workloads that use them. That need for expertise is unlikely to stop; companies will undergo changes in AI strategy as they get to grips with a still-evolving technology.
From the desk to the datacenter

ASUS expects this AI surge to continue in the datacenter, but elsewhere too, specifically in edge locations (especially industrial use cases) and at developers' desks, as the applications that will power the enterprise get made. It wants to be top of peoples' list for hardware and services at all these places along the AI continuum.
At NVIDIA's GTC show in Berlin on Oct 21-22, it announced a full-stack AI offering that it's calling its Enterprise Agentic AI Solution. It's three-layer affair, featuring:
ASUS AI Server and Infrastructure: Its selection of AI servers, including several new units.
ASUS AI Software Stack: Its software for integrating and controlling AI workflows.
ASUS AI HUB: A services operation that ties it all together.

These bring together some existing assets that ASUS had for enterprise AI users, along with some new ones. The time is right for an end-to-end offering with new hardware because of the way the market is shifting, say ASUS execs.

"ASUS servers help enterprises build high-performance agentic AI infrastructure capable of supporting both complex task execution and large-scale AI agent deployment, accelerating enterprise adoption of agentic AI," says Paul Ju, senior vice president and head of infrastructure solution BG at ASUS.
While generative AI initially spiked demand, the advent of agentic AI has sent compute demand into overdrive. Ju explains that the focus is expanding from the GPU.

"Historically, AI servers have been optimized primarily around GPU compute. But as enterprise AI shifts toward agentic AI, workloads increasingly revolve around a continuous ‘agent loop’ that is heavily CPU-dependent," he says. That loop takes in task planning, code execution, external tool invocation, and reflection or correction work.
The CPU's increased role in this execution work is creating bottlenecks in conventional AI servers, he adds.

The first such sticking point is single-thread performance, which leaves GPUs idling while they wait for CPUs to complete. The second lies in memory bandwidth. When this is managed on a per-core basis, it can slow things down when many agents run at once.

The multi-die design of many CPUs also penalizes them in AI environments, because accessing data across dies introduces latency, Ju argues. CPUs with cores and cache on different dies suffer latency when data has to cross between them. Maintaining cache coherency exacerbates that problem.
Finally, there's a security risk: a lack of hardware level sandbox isolation on some CPUs make it possible for prompt injection to reach core systems, he warns.

Customers also bring their own challenges as they grapple with different applications for AI. Enterprises evaluating AI server options have to match their server platforms to the projected AI workload profiles, Ju adds. Training a supervised learning model to batch-classify insurance claims takes different technical resources to running a low-latency reasoning employee chatbot.
What ASUS took to Berlin
ASUS wants to help customers solve problems like these wherever they come up. With this in mind, the company had plenty of goodies for onlookers at GTC.

Starting at the datacenter, the company announced both single and full-rack systems built around the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 eight-GPU server board. It has a 3U hybrid-cooled system, the XA NR11-E12L, along with the 2U 100 percent liquid-cooled XA NR11-E12, both targeting large AI reasoning workloads.

The two Rubin units target different use cases. The 3U hybrid liquid cooling system uses direct-to-chip liquid cooling on the 8GPU baseboard, along with air-cooled dual Xeon 6 chips on a sled. The company pegs this as the easy transition path into AI factory hardware. The 2U unit, with its 100 percent liquid cooling, is tailored for maximum PUE and compute density. It also uses a cable-free board-to-board design to keep its footprint low.
The kit will be speedy, too, with NVIDIA HGX Rubin offering 800Gbit of integrated bandwidth per GPU.

ASUS is promoting the serviceability of these units through their use of tool list CPU and GPU sleds. It claims up to a 50 percent time saving on maintenance operations for these units, meaning less downtime per service and ultimately a lower total cost of ownership.
Delivered fast for NVIDIA HGX Rubin

ASUS is structuring its hardware proposition around speedy delivery so that customers can get hardware up and running to support their AI initiatives. That speed comes from validation carried out before delivery with the help of a pre-validated rack reference architecture.
NVIDIA MGX Server for flexible builds

In keeping with its focus on multiple designs for the right AI workload, ASUS also supports NVIDIA's modular MGX Blueprint for server builds. The selling point here is flexibility with a mixture of GPUs, CPUs, and networking options for enterprise inference, agents, and visual computing. This is the modular route for workloads that don't need the power of an 8-GPU HGX baseboard, and it covers a large gamut of enterprise inference and agentic use cases.

ASUS showcased MGX servers including the 6U XA P8A-E14AXL with its eight liquid-cooled NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. A 2U sibling, the XA P4N-E2, sports NVIDIA Vera processors for agentic work.
Solutions for the edge and developers

The ASUS booth also featured the ExpertCenter Pro ET900N G3, powered by the GB300 Grace Blackwell Superchip developer desktop with 748GB of coherent memory, and the Ascent GX10 based on NVIDIA DGX Spark for agentic work. Also on show were the ProArt GR1X Mini PC and ProArt P16 and P14 laptop - the first laptops powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark - aimed at both developers and creators.

For edge installations, it showed the PE3000N, its rugged NVIDIA Jetson T5000-based edge-AI computer aimed at use cases including industrial environments. Announced a year ago, this delivers up to 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS of peak AI performance with 128GB of memory. Targeted at industrial AI environments was the PE6000G, a workstation-grade AI and simulation platform.
Rehearsing the AI factory in a digital twin

Equipment only supports an AI factory when there is power to run it. ASUS has been taking steps with NVIDIA as a partner here, adopting its DSX AI Factory platform with digital twin system for laying out hardware and power in AI factory environments. DSX supports equipment using the NVIDIA Vera Rubin processor line, which supports dry coolers and a lower PUE with a 45 degree centigrade warm water inlet.

ASUS configured racks become simulation-ready assets inside DSX, adopting its OpenUSD shared file format. That covers engineering data alongside the geometry for measuring real power draw and cooling requirements.

ASUS wanted to target cooling as part of the original design plan for the AI Factory, not as a facility afterthought. So, the DSX partnership allows implementation teams to model water temperature, flow, pressure, CDU placement, and piping within the digital twin model. They translate information from the planning resources that go around this, such as the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint framework, using the ASUS Infrastructure Deployment Center.
Faster to build, easier to run

The digital twin system isn't just for design and setup. It's supposed to keep working after go-live so that AI factory operators can simulate changes before touching hardware. The ASUS Control Center monitors the infrastructure while DSX exchange links IT and operational technology data. Operators can validate changes in the simulation before flipping the switch to go live.

ASUS' goal here is clear: to assist enterprise customers as they tackle in-house AI opportunities while acknowledging that the performance profile and physical locations of their workloads will vary. As companies continue to evolve their understanding of AI and where it fits within the organization, they will need to be agile in how they plan and nurture their infrastructure from the datacenter out to the edge, and to the developer's desk.
The Berlin announcements tie it together in a neat package for organizations that need help with their agentic aspirations.

8db2741ae46b2d45: PETALING JAYA: Kesediaan Barisan Nasional (BN) menawarkan jawatan kepada Perikatan Nasional (PN) dalam pentadbiran Melaka jika menang PRN dilihat sebagai 'pelaburan politik' jangka panjang bagi membina kerjasama lebih kukuh menjelang PRU16, kata penganalisis.

“Ia juga isyarat persefahaman BN-PN bukan sekadar kerjasama pilihan raya tetapi berpotensi berkembang menjadi perkongsian kuasa dalam pentadbiran,” kata ahli akademik daripada Universiti Malaya kepada FMT.

Mazlan Ali daripada Universiti Teknologi Malaysia pula berkata, walaupun BN mempunyai kekuatan untuk menguasai Melaka dan membentuk Kerajaan tunggal, kerjasama dengan PN penting dalam percaturan lebih besar menghadapi PRU16.
Katanya, BN mahu memanfaatkan pengaruh PN khususnya PAS bagi membantu mobilisasi pengundi Melayu dan memberi kelebihan kepada Umno ketika parti itu berdepan beberapa isu seperti kontroversi.
Menurutnya, ia termasuk berkait Lembaga Tabung Haji dan derma untuk membayar denda bekas perdana menteri Najib Razak yang menjadi syarat pengampunan bersyaratnya.
"Ia telah menggugat keyakinan orang Melayu…dan Umno perlu sokongan PN untuk mengekalkan undi mereka," katanya.
Mazlan berkata, keinginan Umno mengekalkan naratif 'perpaduan ummah', yang menurutnya sukar dijayakan tanpa PAS juga mendorong kerjasama itu terjalin.
“Di Melaka, Zahid buka ruang kepada PN bagi menjaga hubungan ke masa depan,” katanya.
36d4af5b6e476e47: From Clement Stanley
Malaysian Indian People’s Party, a Perikatan Nasional component, decided to skip the Melaka state election as a matter of principle, or so they say.
MIPP president P Punithan said the party would not compromise its principles simply to secure seats in the Nov 14 polls.

MIPP’s struggle, he declares, is to defend the interests of the Indian community with dignity and principles, and “that the community’s voice and interests deserve proper recognition and representation in the political landscape”.
In short, MIPP likely does not want to be seen as token for the opposition coalition’s supposed inclusiveness.
Which, in essence is fine. After all, how can a party market itself as an outfit that champions the Indian cause when it finds itself marginalised?
It is just horrible branding — apart from the fact they lost their deposits in the Johor election — which could be a factor as to why seat negotiations failed.
Yet, MIPP’s dilemma is also, to a certain extent, MIC’s.
What role does MIC play in the bigger scheme of things with respect to its affiliation with Barisan Nasional?
Would MIC be willing to accept the fact that it is by and large irrelevant and a “diversity hire” of sorts?
Are they content being pliant to Umno, BN’s lynchpin, since such an arrangement may guarantee a government post?
Or will they only display bravado, via empty threats to quit BN, before the party’s AGM?
To MIPP’s credit, they were brave to acknowledge where they stand in PN. It is now time for the MIC to do the same.
Pliancy and bravado, however, also bring us to MCA.
Mocked as being Umno’s lapdog for the longest time, MCA leaders walked out of BN’s candidate announcement over seat allocations, also over principles.

The party, its president Wee Ka Siong said, cannot be pushed around and deserves to be treated with dignity. Wee also later called out BN chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi on his claim that talks held after the walkout were “positive”.
Whether one believes it was just “wayang kulit”, the bravado eventually secured three seats for MCA to contest at the Melaka election.
But can MCA consider this a win?
The optics will definitely boost its morale.
Perhaps this will give MCA something to build on. Perhaps they believe that by riding on the tailcoats of a BN-PN pact they will win over more Chinese support for the party.
But truth be told, their victory would be somewhat hollow if they won based on the support of the non-Chinese voters.
Be that as it may, MCA must surely know they are no force to be reckoned with amongst the Chinese electorate.
But, if survival is the name of the game, then by all means be indebted to the Malay support for putting them back in a position of power in Johor, Negeri Sembilan and now very likely, in Melaka.
MCA now need only ask themselves, “How high?” when told to jump by the likes of Umno and PAS.
Clement Stanley is an FMT reader.

6f3018cb63f5192e: PETALING JAYA: Malaysian cinema has never lacked variety, but several local productions arriving this season are looking beyond familiar formulas.
One draws on Hungry Ghost Festival traditions, another puts persons with disabilities at the heart of an underwater adventure, while a third centres three deaf teenagers from different backgrounds.
Together, they show how filmmakers are using genre, culture and lived experience to tell stories that feel distinctly Malaysian.
1. ‘Lunar July’ turns Ghost Month traditions into folk horror
Showing in cinemas as of press time, “Lunar July” takes inspiration from the seventh lunar month and the beliefs and customs surrounding the Hungry Ghost Festival.
Directed by JeRR PS Rion, the film incorporates familiar elements such as getai performances and Da Shi Ye, the guardian figure associated with wandering spirits during the month.
The story follows a city rock band invited to perform at a Hungry Ghost Festival celebration in a village, where trouble begins after members of the group dismiss local taboos and offend Da Shi Ye.

For JeRR, however, the film did not begin as a straightforward ghost story. He has said the idea grew from time spent backstage at a Hungry Ghost Festival performance, where he became increasingly interested in the rituals, stories and beliefs surrounding the event.

The project was originally conceived as a comedy before evolving into a supernatural production. Rather than use the traditions purely as horror decoration, JeRR said he wanted to explore the cultural meaning behind them and challenge simplistic perceptions of Da Shi Ye as merely a frightening figure.

That gives “Lunar July” a recognisably Malaysian cultural foundation: getai stages, offerings and the idea of unseen audiences are not simply visual props, but part of a larger set of beliefs connected with remembrance, compassion and respect for the dead.

The Hungry Ghost Festival is traditionally observed during the seventh lunar month, when spirits are believed to be able to wander among the living. Performances may be staged for both human and unseen audiences, with front-row seats sometimes deliberately left empty.

For audiences unfamiliar with these traditions, “Lunar July” therefore offers more than jump scares. It uses horror as a gateway into a part of Malaysian Chinese cultural life that many may have seen from a distance without fully understanding.
2. ‘The Last Dive’ puts disabled performers beneath the surface

Due in cinemas on Dec 3, “The Last Dive” ("Takdir Terakhir") approaches representation from a very different angle. Inspired by a true story, the film features five persons with disabilities performing their own underwater diving scenes rather than relying on visual effects to recreate the action.

Executive producer Wendy Wong told Bernama that the performers brought their own experiences to the production, and were there not to invite sympathy but to demonstrate what they were capable of doing.
The film follows Faiz, a former footballer who becomes paralysed after a hit-and-run accident, and Amelia, a scuba instructor who helps persons with disabilities experience the underwater world.
Around 90% of filming took place at Pulau Lang Tengah and Pulau Bidong in Terengganu, with cast and crew involved in underwater scenes undergoing training and obtaining diving licences.

The idea was inspired by a story Wong heard about a woman with terminal cancer who used a wheelchair and wanted to experience diving before she died. Although her mobility was limited on land, she reportedly felt a sense of freedom underwater.

The production also carries an environmental message touching on marine pollution, fish bombing and coral theft, while highlighting the damage rubbish can cause to turtles and other marine life. Click here to watch the trailer.
In May, "The Last Dive" was screened at a special event in Cannes, France, followed by a screening in Beijing in September.
3. ‘Sayang Sayang’ finds connection across difference
Opening in Malaysian cinemas today, “Sayang Sayang” follows three deaf teenagers from different ethnic backgrounds as they navigate family relationships and the desire to be understood.

Directed by Taiwan’s Tang Hsiang-Chu and produced by Jin Ong, the Malaysian-Taiwanese collaboration was filmed along the coastlines of Kelantan and Terengganu and has earned five nominations at the 63rd Golden Horse Awards.

FMT Lifestyle previously examined the film’s approach to deaf representation and Malaysia’s multicultural identity. Here, it serves as another example of local cinema looking beyond conventional protagonists and giving greater space to experiences that are often underrepresented onscreen.

These three titles differ sharply in tone - supernatural, adventurous and intimate - but each draws its strength from stories rooted close to home, demonstrating novel ways to tell tales that deserve to be told.
f1b542b5d0d2c37d: WASHINGTON: Has MAGA fever finally broken? Will the American right shed Donald Trump's populist ideology and return to more traditional conservatism?
After a resounding defeat in midterm elections that were all about one man, many Republicans on Wednesday are questioning the party's future - and the role, if any, of president Trump in shaping it.

The Wall Street Journal, whose opinion pages are the standard-bearer of the establishment right, has demanded "soul-searching" and called for a break with the ultranationalist, identity-based rhetoric that fuelled the octogenarian's rise to power.

"Tariffs and mass deportation are no substitute for rising real incomes. Playing to the bro MAGA base is no substitute for persuading Hispanics, independents and suburban swing voters who abandoned the party on Tuesday," the Journal's editorial board wrote Wednesday morning.
'Still your president'
The White House was in a less reflective mood.
Its first X post Wednesday featured a stern-looking Trump with the words "Trump is still your president" superimposed on it - a reminder he can remain in office until January 2029.
But the American political cycle is relentless. Wednesday effectively marks the kickoff of the 2028 campaign, which will culminate in a vote on Trump's successor.
And in this race, Trump is out for good, since the US Constitution bars him from seeking a third term.
There was no plausible scenario in which Trump would have emerged from the midterms in a stronger position.
But the absolute thrashing Republicans took Tuesday night - far outpacing all but the most optimistic scenarios for Democrats - has accelerated Trump's loss of power.
Eyes on 2028
In an essay-length X post Wednesday, vice president JD Vance - a likely 2028 White House contender - took care to avoid confrontation with his boss.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote, immediately adding: "The president himself said so last night."
That is not entirely true. Trump only partially blamed the Middle East conflict for the defeat. He also said Republicans fielded poor candidates.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis described an "extinction-level event" for Republicans and thinks they may have to wait until 2032 to regain control of Congress.
The party "needs to reclaim our Reagan principles," Republican lawmaker Don Bacon wrote on X. "Voters rejected populism, chaos, Putin and tariffs."

Former congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, a far-right figure who now fiercely and publicly opposes the president, said, "If the GOP wants any chance in the future, it will have to kick Donald Trump out of the party."
"Republicans need to get back to basics," Matthew Boyle, a leading figure at far-right news site Breitbart, wrote on X.
"No more endless wars... When it comes to the economy, the number one issue, pursue policies that help ordinary people not special interests," he added. "And be sane with immigration enforcement."
Criticism, not by name
But for now, the criticism remains relatively muted. Few conservative figures, whether moderate or radical, have attacked Trump by name.
The Republican Party has, after all, tied its fate entirely to the billionaire since 2016.

"The big question is, are some of these Republican leaders in the House and Senate going to distance themselves from Trump?" Amy Dacey, a former Democratic official who is now an expert at American University, told AFP.
The same goes for far-right influencers, whose audiences - and incomes - have tracked Trump's popularity.
A stunning loss dings influence, "but this is not going to, in any way, eradicate some people who are affiliated with some of the MAGA movement," Dacey added.
Some of MAGA's digital foot soldiers have tried to redirect the reckoning.
"Great work, neocons," Jack Posobiec wrote sarcastically on X, referring to a Republican faction known for interventionist foreign policy and a hawkish stance against Iran.
But it may only be a matter of time before the break becomes definitive.
Former congressman Bob Good said on the same platform: "Gotta start by acknowledging that Trump was and is the problem. Quietly whispering it won't do it."

a40b144ab5da56eb: From a layperson’s perspective, following the legal back-and-forth in the Malaysian courts can be rather taxing.
It often appears to be a war of words, legal arguments, constitutional interpretations and courtroom strategies, all aimed at persuading the presiding judge or judges.

Beneath the pomp and pageantry inherited from the British legal system, however, lie issues of profound constitutional significance that may or may not affect our lives today, but could have far-reaching consequences for generations to come.

When Malaysia was formed in 1963, several safeguards were negotiated to protect the interests and autonomy of North Borneo (now Sabah). Among these was Point 11 of the Inter-Governmental Committee (IGC) Report, under the heading tariffs and finance.
It provided that “North Borneo should retain control over its own finances, development and tariffs, with the right to formulate its own taxation policies and raise loans on its own credit”.

One can argue that the spirit and substance of this safeguard are found in the constitutional expression of Article 112C of the Federal Constitution, read together with Section 2(1) of Part IV of the Tenth Schedule and Clauses (1), (3) and (4) of Article 112D.

These provisions form the constitutional basis for Sabah's entitlement to a special grant equivalent to two-fifths (40%) of the net revenue derived by the federal government from Sabah, subject to the relevant constitutional provisions.

Former Sabah minister Yap Pak Leong revived the historical significance of this arrangement, maintaining that the 40% revenue-sharing arrangement was a fundamental condition underpinning Sabah's decision to join in the formation of Malaysia.
"Right from the start, I emphasised this share of 2/5 revenue to be a condition for Sabah to become part of Malaysia.”
He further stressed that without this safeguard being enshrined in the Federal Constitution, Sabah would not have agreed to participate in the formation of Malaysia.

The role Sabah and Sarawak played in forming Malaysia must be recognised, unlike the federated states of Malaya. The Borneo states negotiated separate terms under the IGC, one of which is Sabah’s entitlement to 40% revenue sharing of all taxes collected in Sabah.

From what I understand, the federal government is not objecting to Sabah’s right to the 40% revenue sharing, but to the High Court judgment on Oct 17, 2025, in favour of the Sabah Law Society (SLS), directing the federal and state government to commence a review within a stipulated period.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim himself promised during the last state election that the government would not appeal the High Court’s decision, but for whatever reasons, it seems he has reneged on that promise to the Sabah people.
On another point, one cannot help but question the position taken by the state government in these proceedings.
Having entered the case as an intervener at a relatively late stage, the state government appears caught between competing legal and political considerations.
Yet, arguably, it should have been at the forefront pursuing Sabah's constitutional entitlement.
The state government possesses the political mandate, institutional authority and constitutional standing to negotiate directly with the federal government.

Rather than allowing the matter to become an extended courtroom battle initiated by SLS on behalf of the people of Sabah, it should be exercising that authority to secure a meaningful and just resolution for Sabah's 47 "lost years".

In another case, another NGO, Sabah Action Body Advocating Rights (Sabar) has taken the federal government to court on February 27, 2025, disputing the validity of the Territorial Sea Act (TSA) 2012, which limits the State's maritime boundary to just three nautical miles.

While the Sabah state government may have its own reasons for not initiating legal challenges regarding Sabah's rights, and Sabahans are not privy to their arguments, it is only fair to ask where the Sabah government stands in relation to these key court challenges.
The position is unlike in Sarawak, where the state government has led similar challenges.

Importantly, after more than six decades since Sabah agreed to become a part of Malaysia, one uncomfortable reality remains: according to official statistics, Sabah continues to record the highest poverty incidence in the country.
That is a sobering indictment of the development gap that persists despite Sabah's immense natural resources and its contributions to the Malaysian federation.
The legal arguments may continue. Appeals may be filed, constitutional provisions may be debated, and lawyers may argue over jurisdiction, procedures and remedies.
But beyond the courtroom, ordinary Sabahans continue to face the realities of poverty, inadequate infrastructure, water and electricity shortages, and limited economic opportunities.

The fundamental question is this: after more than 60 years in the Malaysian federation, should Sabahans still have to fight in court for constitutional assurances that were meant to protect their interests from the very beginning?

The 40% entitlement should not be treated as a political bargaining chip, nor should its fulfilment be reduced to a battle of legal technicalities. It is a constitutional matter rooted in the historical terms and safeguards surrounding the formation of Malaysia.
It is about justice, constitutional accountability and the future of Sabah.
The people of Sabah have waited long enough. Following Lord Hewart CJ’s well-known dictum, “justice must be seen to be done”.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
e0aa4e6ab2afafa9: Dalam tulisan ini saya ingin mengingatkan diri saya dan orang Melayu Islam yang lain supaya menjaga keimanan agar tidak terjebak dengan perkara yang boleh mengancam kedudukan kita di akhirat nanti.
Ini adalah berkaitan dengan suatu kumpulan orang Melayu Islam yang ‘galak’ sangat menghukum dan menuduh orang bukan Islam rakyat Malaysia sebagai kafir, musuh-musuh Islam dan ejen penjajah.

Dalam pembacaan semua hadis-hadis koleksi saya seperti Sahih Al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abu Dawud dan Al-Muwatta versi terjemahan Inggeris serta juga At-Tirmidzi, An-Nasa’i dan Ibn Majah versi terjemahan Indonesia, saya terserempak dengan suatu hadis yang pada mulanya suatu misteri tetapi akhirnya menjadi pedoman serta ingatan saya sebagai seorang Muslim yang menjiwakan Sunnah Rasulullah dan bukannya perbuatan atau kata-kata ustaz dan agamawan lain:

Sebaliknya, seseorang di antara kalian ada yang beramal dengan amalan ahli syurga sehingga jarak antara dirinya dan syurga tinggal sehasta, lalu takdir mendahuluinya, sehingga ia beramal dengan amalan ahli neraka dan masuklah ia ke dalam neraka." (Hadis Riwayat Bukhari dan Muslim)

Pertama sekali saya berdepan hadis ini adalah versi Inggeris dan saya dapat versi Melayu ini dari internet. Saya amat terkejut apabila dikatakan Rasulullah supaya jangan kita anggap seseorang itu yang berkelakuan seperti orang jahat akan berakhir dengan ia ke neraka dan seorang yang berkelakuan seperti orang baik tidak semestinya berakhir dengan ditempatkan di syurga.

Bagi saya, kalau seorang yang berkelakuan tidak bermoral dan berniat jahat itu mungkin di akhir hayatnya akan menjadi baik kerana bertaubat dan membetulkan kesalahannya itu suatu kemungkinan dan suatu harapan baik.

Tetapi, saya terasa pelik bila merenung macam mana seorang yang ‘baik’ bersembahyang, berjuang atas nama Islam, memimpin parti politik Islam setengah abad ada kemungkinan berakhir di tempat selain syurga?

Saya memang tidak menyangka yang pada suatu hari nanti saya akan melihat dengan mata saya sendiri dan mendengar dengan telinga sendiri tokoh-tokoh Melayu umat Islam yang saya amat hormati dan sayangi mengubah kelakuan mereka 180 darjah menjadi orang yang berkelakuan tidak bermoral dan tidak berperasaan kemanusiaan langsung ketika saya dan mereka masih hidup di dunia ini.

Sejak saya kenal sedikit politik sewaktu umur dua puluhan bermula di Amerika Syarikat saya menjadi lebih matang sewaktu era Reformasi tahun 1998 ketika Anwar Ibrahim dipenjarakan, dimalukan dan dipukul separuh mati daripada orang Melayu Islam kita sendiri.

Pada saya, semua tokoh-tokoh parti ini memang perlu menjadi sanjungan dan ikutan orang Melayu umat Islam kerana kecekalan dan keikhlasan mereka melawan Umno dan Dr Mahathir Mohamad ketika itu.
Ia adalah Melayu lawan Melayu. Melayu Islam melawan Melayu nasionalis. Saya di dalam golongan Melayu Islam dan membenci Melayu nasionalis.

Walaupun kebencian saya terhadap Umno dan Mahathir amat besar sekali, tidak ada sekali pun saya pernah menuduh mereka itu munafik atau kafir atau menjadi ejen penjajah, jauh sekali sebagai musuh-musuh Islam.
Bagi saya perbalahan adalah kepada mereka yang terperangkap dengan konsep Islam tradisi dan Islam institusi maka reformis Islam perlu membebaskan mereka daripada belenggu tersebut.
Saya masih ingat reformis yang mengikuti reformasi tidak pernah membakar gambar tokoh-tokoh Umno atau menuduh mereka munafik serta mempunyai ciri dajal.
Memanglah ada sejarah seorang tokoh dan suatu parti itu mengkafirkan Umno tetapi saya, walaupun menjadi ahli parti tersebut, tidak pernah bersikap demikian.
Saya amat tergamam apabila saya melihat parti yang memperjuangkan Islam sebagai antiasabiyah atau perkauman tiba-tiba bersekongkol dengan parti yang memperjuangkan perkauman Melayu.

Saya berasa terkejut apabila dari lidah tokoh Melayu Islam sendiri terkeluar kata-kata kesat dan menghina kepada kaum bukan Islam serta menuduh kaum Islam lain sebagai bersahabat dengan musuh-musuh Islam dan penjajah.
Saya amat terkejut juga apabila tergamak ahli parti itu membaca Qunut Nazilah ke atas rakyat Malaysia daripada semua kaum dan agama yang menjadi lawan politik mereka.
Dan kini saya juga terkejut tentang lafaz munafik dan dajal yang dilemparkan kepada orang Melayu umat Islam yang berbeza polisi dan pandangan dalam politik.
Lebih teruk lagi parti itu mengutip derma jihad untuk mengiyakan fitnah jelas ahlinya ke atas orang bukan Islam yang lain demi ‘perjuangan menegakkan Islam’ dalam negara.
Kita semua akan meninggalkan dunia ini di akhir hayat kita. Apakah penjelasan kita bila berdepan dengan penghakiman akhirat nanti?
Adakah kita akan bergantung kepada argumen ‘demi perjuangan Islam’ maka any way is the halal way?
Janganlah kita ghairah sangat bertakbir dan bertempik Islam namun tergadai akhirnya iman dan jiwa kita kepada kemunafikan dan pendajjalan diri kita sendiri di akhir hayat nanti.

c6b1da594a8a831d: Over 60% of Floridian voters voted to cut property taxes, which has been surging in recent years. AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)Many Florida homeowners cheered on Nov. 3, 2026, when more than 60% of voters approved a constitutional amendment to significantly reduce property taxes. Under the measure, Amendment 3, a homeowner’s tax break, known as a homestead exemption, would triple from the current US$50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028. By shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation, this exemption effectively lowers homeowners’ tax bills. New homeowners would also reportedly be eligible for a property tax break, but on a more phased-in basis. But the measure comes with a hefty price tag. The Florida Legislature’s research arm estimated the measure would reduce annual revenue from property taxes by $11.8 billion. This translates to a 30% reduction in revenue for Florida counties and a 13% cut for smaller municipal governments. While homeowners will get some relief, the budget crunch due to the lower tax revenue will affect other Floridians in more adverse ways. As economists who have been following the debates over Amendment 3, we argue that local governments will struggle to fund basic services with less money. And we expect more sweeping economic consequences as well – including less affordable residential housing and a broader shift of the tax burden away from relatively wealthier homeowners to those who are less well off. How Amendment 3 would work Much of the political momentum for Amendment 3 came from a rise in the cost of living and frustration over rising property taxes. These now average just over $3,000 annually but can run much higher for Floridians with more expensive homes. In addition to raising the homestead tax exemption, Amendment 3 lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% increase to a 5% increase. Since property taxes are based on an asset’s assessed value, this language effectively limits but doesn’t rule out tax hikes for businesses. So landlords, for example, could still see meaningful annual tax increases as their properties go up in value – costs that would likely be passed on to renters. Amendment 3 makes clear that school-related property taxes are exempt from these tax cuts. It also lists some theoretical limits on how local governments should use tax dollars, as a way to ensure continued funding for essential services such as public safety, infrastructure or obligations for employee retirement benefits. But it also states that funds may be used for “expenditures approved” by local and county governments – ambiguous wording that suggests these stipulations can be breached. Who pays the bill? Florida property taxes are levied and collected by some 640 local government entities. There’s no state income tax, so any reductions in property tax revenue directly affect local and county governments. With tax revenue slashed, businesses, landlords and owners of other non-homestead properties like second homes would almost certainly see their taxes go up. This is a typical pattern: When governments cut property taxes for some groups, taxes shift to other groups. Essential public services, including fire and police departments, could face sharp budget cuts due to the shortfall from lower property taxes. Orange County Fire Rescue Department via AP This dynamic is likely to play out with local governments as they try to keep revenue stable: Amendment 3 would force them to hike taxes in other areas to make up for the shortfall. This could include increases in state and local sales taxes, an expansion of the list of goods subject to sales taxes, or a hike in “documentary stamp taxes,” which are required on documents such as deeds, bonds and mortgages. State and local governments could also impose higher fees for specific services, such as solid waste treatment and stormwater utilities. Another option is to hike permits and inspection fees, fuel taxes or other service charges such as vehicle registration fees. Finally, local governments could raise tourism-related taxes, such as on food, beverages and hotels. But this recourse wouldn’t help counties with limited tourism, and such revenues fluctuate in any event. In the end, though, essential services would still almost certainly be affected. Funding for police, fire and emergency medical services is primarily the responsibility of local governments, and, for most counties, they make up the largest line item in their annual expenditures. Reducing property taxes would amount to a direct hit, especially in smaller, less-populated counties. And if local governments do raise sales tax rates to the extent they can, lower-income Floridians will bear a disproportionate burden as they spend much more of their income on consumption. They’re also far more likely to rent than own a home, so any increased rents would take a bigger toll. A looming affordable housing crunch? Less noticed in the debate over Amendment 3 was how it would affect the state’s affordable housing shortage. We argue that the structure of the property tax cut will likely create more incentives for counties and developers to build commercial structures instead of more residential housing. When developers build residential homes, they require a basic level of public services to support residents and the local infrastructure. In fact, property taxes in much of Florida effectively subsidize residential home development: For every dollar that a homeowner pays in property taxes, it costs county governments around $1.20 to provide those services. This gap will only grow when property tax revenues fall. From the standpoint of local and county governments, then, it may make more sense to focus on commercial or industrial construction as a way to keep tax revenues stable. But with fewer homes built at the expense of business construction – from manufacturing to data centers – the supply squeeze will only drive up prices and rents for the workers who are needed for those jobs. Now that Amendment 3 is on the books, Florida’s county and local governments will confront major trade-offs. We believe that state officials will come to realize how much of a change has been made – and how quickly their priorities may have to shift. e9262ebde8d56524: During World War II, physicists on the Manhattan Project worried that the Nazi German nuclear program might achieve the first nuclear bomb before the US and its allies. That's not what transpired, but historians have debated just how close the Germans came to achieving criticality in their last attempt at building a reactor: the B8 pile. Werner Heisenberg, who led that effort, claimed that they were close and had only needed a little more uranium. But according to a paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences Nexus, that was not the case: the project simply didn't have sufficient uranium and heavy water to build a working bomb, given the design they were using.

This particular research started in 2013, when University of Maryland physicist Timothy Koeth—a co-author on the new paper—received the gift of a mysterious heavy metal cube from a friend. He instantly recognized it as one of the uranium cubes used by German scientists in their unsuccessful attempt to build a working nuclear reactor. Only 14 such cubes are known to exist today.

In 2019, we reported on Koeth’s quest to track down the cube’s origins, as well as several other similar cubes that had somehow found their way across the Atlantic. At the time, Koeth and his partner in the quest, then-graduate student Miriam “Mimi” Hiebert, had tracked down ten such cubes around the US. For instance, the Smithsonian Institute had a German uranium cube in storage. They tracked a third cube to Harvard University, where it was regularly passed around to students in introductory physics classes as a curiosity.

13a4307bdfd76e19: On 25 October 2026, Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured a fourth term in an election that exposed both the resilience of Brazilian democracy and the depth of the far right’s social roots. Lula received 51.79% of valid votes in the runoff against far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.21%. Three weeks earlier, however, the outcome had looked very different: Flávio - son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, now jailed for a coup attempt after losing his bid for reelection in 2022 - led the first round with 47.03% of the valid votes, compared with Lula’s 45.16%. The reversal was not simply an electoral comeback. It revealed how a campaign that had failed to generate enthusiasm could be transformed through collective mobilization, both online and in the streets. The first round result was a warning against complacency. Lula’s campaign leaned heavily on his historical achievements and the restoration of policies associated with his previous Workers’ Party (PT) governments. These accomplishments were real, but they did not necessarily offer a persuasive answer to a question increasingly heard among voters: what comes next? For those who have voted for Lula repeatedly over decades, the promise of continuity could coexist with political fatigue. His age and the campaign’s difficulty in speaking to younger voters added to this sense of exhaustion. Meanwhile, the assumption that Jair Bolsonaro’s imprisonment had removed any serious electoral threat proved dangerously mistaken. A central contradiction was that the defense of social policies did not automatically translate into a sense of economic security. Many households continued to experience the erosion of purchasing power, high borrowing costs and persistent indebtedness. According to a Brazil’s National Confederation of Commerce’s July 2026 survey, 82% of Brazilian families reported outstanding debts, 29.8% had overdue bills, and debt payments absorbed approximately 29.5% of monthly household income. Among families earning up to three times the country’s minimum wage, indebtedness reached 84.9%. The politics of everyday insecurity Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign managed to combine continuity and novelty. His surname preserved his father’s political identity and loyal electorate, while his comparatively younger image, disciplined media performances and lack of experience in the federal Executive allowed him to present himself as an alternative to incumbent Lula. Flávio was not a political outsider: his legislative career was substantial. Yet the campaign’s effectiveness lay in its ability to turn familiar grievances into an apparently new political offer. Public security was especially important in this. Fear of street crime, mobile phone theft and drug trafficking were connected to a broader discourse of order and punishment. The invocation of “narcoterrorism” also resonated with the language of United States’ President Donald Trump administration, demonstrating how domestic electoral agendas are increasingly entangled with geopolitical narratives. The campaign likewise foregrounded supermarket prices, debt and the difficulty saving money. Not every issue was directly within the federal government’s remit, but the political effect was to hold Lula accountable for the totality of everyday insecurity. The territorial pattern of the vote also matters. The first round strength of the far right in rural regions and municipalities in the country’s interior points to the consolidation of what might be called agribusiness linked “Bolsonarismo”. This is not to suggest that agribusiness is politically homogeneous, or that every rural voter supports the far right. Rather, it indicates that a powerful political alignment has taken shape across parts of Brazil’s Center-West, the interior of populous and rich São Paulo state and other areas where export oriented agriculture exercises economic and social influence. Its expansion into new agricultural frontiers, including the “MATOPIBA” region - encompassing parts of Maranhão, Tocantins, Piauí and Bahia states, between the Center-West and Northeast regions of the country - merits systematic electoral and territorial research. “From mourning to struggle” The morning after the first round of the election on October 4 was marked by a profound sense of defeat in Lula’s campaign. Flávio had finished ahead, and the far right had strengthened its institutional presence. The possibility of a return to Bolsonarismo was no longer abstract. Yet, mourning quickly gave way to mobilization. In Portuguese, the transition can be captured in a phrase that is difficult to translate without losing its force: “do luto à luta”, or “from mourning to struggle”. Students took to the streets in Rio de Janeiro state; and soon after marches and smaller neighborhood actions multiplied. Artists, musicians, trade unions and people with little previous experience of organized politics joined demonstrations, leafleting, cultural events and local conversations. It was not merely a sequence of large political rallies. Its significance lay in the diffusion of political activity into everyday spaces: campuses, homes, cultural centers, workplaces and neighborhood networks. Lula’s campaign gained more capillarity, extending beyond the formal structures of parties and electoral committees. Digital mobilization developed in parallel. Influencers urged supporters to remain active, and a WhatsApp channel created by Brazilian congressman André Janones - “Lula’s Army” - provided a recognizable language for coordinated social media campaigning. Supporters exchanged practical guidance about posting, sharing and the unintended consequences of amplifying adversarial content. The far right had long invested in these techniques. What was striking in the runoff was the left’s rapid appropriation of similar forms of distributed communication. But the most important innovation was not technological. It was political. Online networks and street mobilization reinforced one another. Digital messages brought people into public spaces, while visible demonstrations gave online activism a sense of momentum and legitimacy. In a fragmented media environment, neither the street nor the screen was sufficient on its own. A democratic front beyond the left A further condition of Lula’s comeback was the recognition that the traditional right and Bolsonarismo were not identical. The runoff brought together figures with very different political histories, including liberal economists, conservative public personalities and people who had opposed previous Workers’ Party governments. The appeal was not that everyone should become a Lula supporter. It was that defending the possibility of political disagreement required preventing an authoritarian political project from returning to Executive power. This distinction mattered because anti-PT sentiment remained deeply rooted among parts of the Brazilian electorate. Asking voters to endorse Lula’s entire record would have narrowed the coalition. Asking them to defend democratic institutions, even while disagreeing with Lula, opened a broader space. Such a front is necessarily contradictory: its members do not share a single economic program or social vision. Yet, this plurality was its democratic strength along the runoff. Policy debates also returned to the foreground. Proposals to end the six days on, one day off work schedule and move toward a 40 hour work week without wage reductions helped connect democratic mobilization to material demands. Income tax relief, minimum wage increases, protection for app workers such as Uber, social transfers and assistance to small entrepreneurs formed part of the wider political debate. These initiatives differed considerably in legal status: some reflected existing programs, others pending legislation or campaign commitments. What they did show was the importance of linking a defense of democracy to the conditions of working class life. Lula ultimately won more than 64 million votes, reversing the first round defeat. This victory should not be romanticized as the achievement of any single party leader, digital strategy or government announcement. It emerged from an exceptional convergence of political organization, public engagement and the formation of a broader democratic coalition. The economic limits of political victory Winning the election did not resolve the structural tensions facing a fourth Lula administration. The financial market reaction to the result underscored the distance between electoral expectations and investor preferences, while renewed demands for fiscal adjustment raised the prospect of conflict over the government’s social commitments. The central question is whether a government elected through a popular mobilization can maintain and expand social protections under a policy regime that prioritizes expenditure restraint and monetary credibility. The benchmark interest rate stood at 13.75% a year following Brazil’s Central Bank’s September 2026 decision. Orthodox interpretations emphasize fiscal credibility, expectations and debt sustainability, arguing that restraint on primary spending can create conditions for lower rates. Critical and heterodox interpretations stress how persistently high real interest rates can themselves fuel debt accumulation, potentially making austerity economically and socially self defeating. The original Brazilian constitutional spending ceiling introduced under President Michel Temer in 2016 was replaced by a new fiscal framework in 2023. That institutional change matters, but it did not eliminate the political struggle over fiscal limits. The risk for Lula is that accommodating market demands through cuts to social expenditure could undermine the very constituencies whose mobilization secured his victory. Conversely, an ambitious social agenda without a strategy for managing financing conditions and political opposition would face significant obstacles. Democracy, geopolitics and the unfinished struggle Three additional challenges will shape next Lula’s administration. The first is the resilience of the “Bolsonarismo” movement. The presidential defeat did not dissolve its electorate, networks or institutional influence. The far right remains capable of organizing around security, moral conflict and dissatisfaction with living standards. A democratic victory at the ballot box is therefore not the same as the political defeat of authoritarianism. The second is public security. Treating violence exclusively as a state level matter is increasingly untenable when national electoral politics and international narratives of “narcoterrorism” shape the debate. A progressive response must address genuine insecurity without reproducing punitive approaches that disproportionately affect poorer and racialized communities. This will require a social as well as an institutional agenda. The third is geopolitical autonomy. Brazil will have to negotiate with the Trump administration over trade and tariffs while deepening economic relations with China and maintaining a commitment to diversified South–South partnerships. These objectives are not automatically incompatible, but their reconciliation will become harder as competition between major global power intensifies. The question is whether Brazil can defend its policy space and development priorities without being forced into an exclusive alignment. The lesson of the October 2026 elections in Brazil is thus both hopeful and sobering. Collective mobilization can change the course of an election, even when the political atmosphere appears exhausted and defeat seems inevitable. But the energy that makes an electoral comeback possible must confront structures that do not disappear on election night: entrenched economic power, social inequality, geopolitical pressure and the organized strength of the far right. The transition from mourning to struggle was decisive for Lula’s victory. Whether that struggle can also expand democracy’s social and economic foundations is the question that now remains. d482131a72d52e06: As of Tuesday, developers can explore expanded Siri AI integration for their Apple platform apps through beta releases of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3. Next spring, nearly three years after announcing plans for deeper third-party Siri integration, Apple expects to begin accepting App Store submissions using the new capabilities.

"This developer beta offers a sneak peek at Siri AI app intents for developers," Apple said in a developer news post. "With this early Developer Preview, your app can work directly with Siri AI, giving you a first look at new ways to reach and serve your customers."

Anything is likely to be an improvement. Apple's Siri, a voice-activated assistant service, dates back to 2011 and gained limited third-party app access in 2016. In 2024, it became an interface for interacting with Apple Intelligence, its suite of generative AI features.

Apple Intelligence has not been very intelligent – several advertised Siri capabilities were delayed, so much so that Apple was sued in 2025 over allegations of misleading marketing. After a shakeup of Apple's machine learning group in December 2025, Siri and Apple Intelligence received a makeover at Apple's Worldwide Developers Conference in June.

"Before this year, Siri was a timer with a voice," said Roberto Gutierrez, Apple platforms staff engineer at a media company and author of the e-book On-Device Intelligence, in an email to The Register. "Weather, alarms, calls. Anything past that was a coin toss.

"On the developer side, SiriKit covered a handful of domains and Shortcuts only worked if users memorized the phrase. Siri AI is the first version that understands context and can chain actions across apps. That's a real change."

There is a catch, however, Gutierrez observed. Siri AI is available in a limited number of languages and regions. Support for Traditional Chinese is expected by the end of 2026, and EU availability remains a matter of negotiation – Siri AI is unavailable on iOS, iPadOS, and watchOS in the bloc as Apple works through interoperability concerns under Europe's Digital Markets Act.
"Apple is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward," the company said last month without committing to any concessions.
Gutierrez said that he expects opening Siri to third-party developers will be useful to some extent.

"Siri can only do what apps expose through App Intents, and SiriKit is on its way out," he said. "If your app's main actions aren't exposed, the new Siri can't see you. The bigger shift is letting Claude, Gemini and others plug in. Developers already choose between three options for every AI feature: Apple's system model, an open model through MLX, or a cloud API. Siri is heading the same way. It doesn't need to be the smartest model. It needs to be the best router. That's the right call."
Apple has made choosing between those three options more difficult by failing to publish benchmarks that show how its Foundation Models compare with open-weight alternatives.

The biz has published measurements of how its third-generation Foundation Models compare to their 2025 predecessors. But the company's commitment – to "[share] more details on our latest foundation models, including updated evaluations and benchmarks, in a technical report later this summer" – remains unfulfilled so far as we're aware.
Gutierrez ran his own benchmarks to compare Apple's iOS system model (FM system, ~3B) to several open-weight models that are suitable for use on-device.

"On an A17 Pro iPhone running iOS 26, I tested Apple's system model against Qwen3 1.7B and 4B, Llama 3.2 3B and Gemma 3 4B on a structured-output task," he said. "Speed: Apple's model ran at about 149 tok/s, roughly 3x the fastest open model (Qwen3 1.7B, about 46)."
Quality, he said, was a tie, with every model passing five typed checks. But memory, he said, was where Apple's models had an advantage.

"The system model's weights live outside your app's memory budget," he explained. "My app peaked at 12 MB during inference. An open 4B model costs 2.4-2.7 GB, and a 2.4 GB model plus your app plus a WebView is a crash report. So yes, it's competitive, and on iPhone it's the default I'd recommend. If you want your own model, Qwen3 1.7B is the one."

But Gutierrez urged Apple to publish proper competitive benchmarks. "Their numbers compare against their own previous models," he said. "Developers aren't choosing between Apple 2025 and Apple 2026. We're choosing between Apple, Qwen and a cloud API. I had to build my own harness to answer a question Apple could settle with one table."
The absence of competitive model metrics is not the only gap. Apple has also failed to accommodate web apps.

"Web apps are locked out," said Gutierrez. "Foundation Models is a Swift API (and now Python). No JavaScript, no WebKit. A PWA's only option is to ship its own model into the browser and pay the full memory bill inside a WebView."

And bringing your own model may pose performance problems. "On an A17 Pro iPhone, the 3-4B open models pushed the phone into 'fair' thermal state and dropped to 12-24 tok/s," he said. "In practice, your own model on iPhone means ~2B or smaller."

With Siri AI unavailable on iPhones, iPads, and Apple Watches in the EU (and its rollout in mainland China subject to regulatory requirements), developers may need a fallback for global apps to handle regional restrictions. Apple's Private Cloud Compute offers eligible developers access to Foundation Models, Gutierrez observed, though it requires membership in the App Store Small Business Program, fewer than two million first-time App Store downloads across their apps, and the necessary entitlement. ®

eeff4737bf340d02: Voters respond to economic and political messages and experiences. AP Photo/Lindsey WassonAs Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “It’s the economy, stupid.” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy, making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise. Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C. Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think, because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers, with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on. When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food, follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally. Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection. For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record. Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections. Oil embargo, Nixon and Ford Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month, and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32%. When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12.3%, and gas prices were still high. Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “Whip Inflation Now,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats. “WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter. Carter’s struggles In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly. Inflation hit 9% in 1978. In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats. Inflation continued to climb, and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976. Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan. Reagan enters the picture Reagan implemented “Reaganomics” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum. By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut, lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs. In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate. Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate. Trump’s first round In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22%. In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate. Democratic Party supporters react to the results of the 2018 midterm elections, when their party won control of the U.S. House of Representatives. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images Biden years Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40%. Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups. And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon. Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies. Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon. But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord, under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source. In June 2022, inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4.929 per gallon; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today. The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots. Trump’s second term During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4.5%, U.S. oil production rose 3.3%, from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, from $3.12 to $2.98 per gallon. On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Initially, shipment volume plummeted, though by the end of September it had recovered to 82% to 92% of prewar levels. Overall, Middle Eastern crude oil exports are averaging around 24 million barrels a day, exceeding prewar levels in part because of increased use of pipelines out of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Because of the war with Iran, AAA’s national average price of unleaded regular gasoline has increased by almost 40%, from February’s $2.98 price to $4.15 a gallon as of Nov. 3, 2026. Implications As the preelection polling had suggested, voters held Trump accountable for high gasoline and grocery prices, as well as an unpopular war. It was a reminder of a basic economic and political principle: When the economy is doing well, voters are more likely to support incumbents and their parties. And when voters are pessimistic about the economy’s future, they are inclined to vote against incumbents and their parties. Michael A. Mische does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

938f3cec510e6579: Fedora 45 is here, after not one but two week-long delays as the team found last-minute issues. Although both the original and second announcements were irksomely non-specific, in general we prefer this "when it's ready" approach to the rigid calendar-based schedule that Canonical favors for Ubuntu. It includes six main editions, five immutable desktop variants, and 12 "spins" with different GUIs.

The combined version 45 release notes detail some of the bigger individual component changes and note the hardware requirements. The recommended spec is now a 2 GHz quad-core CPU with 8 GB of RAM and 20 GB of disk space, and at least 1024×768 graphics. Fedora 45 supports most display adapters, but 3D acceleration may not work on older GPUs, including Intel models prior to GMA9xx, Nvidia models prior to NV30 (GeForce FX5xxx series), and AMD Radeon models prior to R300 (Radeon 9500).

We took a quick look at the beta back in September, focusing on its new next-generation text console, which is a welcome change. We especially liked the ability to zoom in and out on the text console on the fly, which is something we've missed since the superb "Laptop Ultravision" for DOS, about a third of a century ago. (The company is long gone, but we found a downloadable version for all you DOS users.)

The desktop flagship editions are Workstation 45, which comes with GNOME 51 "A Coruña", and Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop, with KDE Plasma 6.8. We covered some of the new features in GNOME 51 when we looked at the Ubuntu 26.10 beta, and those changes apply here too – notably, improvements in the Settings app, but removal of some older Nvidia GPU support.

Both the big names are Wayland-only environments now, but by our reckoning, X11 fans have seven of the 12 official spins to choose from: Xfce, Cinnamon, MATE, i3, LXQt, LXDE, and Sugar (SOAS) all still use X.org if you prefer. There is also a combined What's New page for all the Atomic Desktops, Fedora’s immutable variants – the main shared feature here being the new web-based installer.

The new version of main Fedora is accompanied by Fedora Asahi Remix 45 for Apple Silicon Macs. This is a more notable release than the cross-platform editions, as Asahi 45 brings initial support for M3-based Macs as well as M1 and M2 kit. As The Reg described in September, though, the M3 support is preliminary and limited – for instance, it excludes the M3 Ultra. If you have an M3 Mac, for now, you're better off sticking to macOS.

The most important changes in Fedora 45 are under the hood, which is what the Red Hat release announcement focuses on. It now uses RPM version 6.1, with enhanced package signature checking, and blocks the vendor of packages silently changing. The GNOME keyring now uses the oo7 secrets manager. Support for two old VPN plugins has been removed, because the packages were unmaintained.

A feature that we are happy to see land at last is better support for Red Hat’s Stratis next-generation storage subsystem. We gave a potted overview of Stratis 3.3 back in 2022: it was on version 3.3 back then. It’s the same main Stratis version 3.9 we saw in Fedora 44, but the installation program now has support for installing Fedora 45 on Stratis storage.

Stratis is Red Hat’s rival to OpenZFS. The plan is that Stratis offers similar features and resilience to ZFS, especially in the field of copy-on-write snapshots and simple multi-device logical volume management, but built from all-GPL code. Rather than a whole new filesystem, Stratis integrates XFS, LVM, and the kernel device-mapper functionality. Stratis 1.0 appeared in Fedora 29 eight years ago, and Fedora 45 has version 3.9.3. It's good to see it finally making real progress: if nothing else, we've seen Btrfs irretrievably corrupt a full volume far too many times to ever trust it again, so an alternative is very welcome.

When we looked at Fedora 44, we noted the difficulty of doing custom disk partitioning. It was there, but very well-hidden. Now, the installer can launch the Cockpit web-management tool to make it easier to set up your drives however you want.

An interesting side-effect of the delayed release is that Fedora 45 ships with kernel 7.2 – specifically, version 7.2.15, which is the last release of this short-term series. In other words, it’s an end-of-life kernel version. It’s an amusing contrast to its near-contemporary Ubuntu 26.10, which shipped with a pre-release kernel. Our test Ubuntu box was automatically upgraded to the release version by the background automatic updates process, but to our surprise, it didn't receive the kernel update for over a week. This shouldn't be a problem: unlike Ubuntu, Fedora releases routinely receive updates to whole new kernel versions, so we’re sure Fedora 45 users will get kernel 7.3 very soon.

We upgraded the same test machine on which we tried GNOME 48 in Fedora 42 early last year. You can skip one Fedora release on upgrade, but not two, so we had to go via Fedora 44 — which took some time, and threw up a minor packaging glitch, but it got there. The result runs surprisingly well, although this 2008 machine is well below the recommended spec. ®

At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities, began changing course himself.

Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.

The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium.

That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.

The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects.

Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it.
A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.

It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.

This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.

Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.
