a312adbc2b5e0af7: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.

Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution—a sort of moral code.
The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions, and mislead their evaluators.

Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage.

An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay.

In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.

A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).

Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.

The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.

A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?”

Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.

During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.

There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.

Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.

Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.”

One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.

It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.

“Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior.

Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.)

Whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” says Hazan. A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it?

“It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he says of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.

a1bb83c79c172522: HONG KONG, Nov 3 — Asian stock markets struggled Tuesday following another AI-fuelled tech selloff on Wall Street that overshadowed a possible breakthrough in talks to end the Middle East war.
However, oil prices clawed back some of Monday’s plunge in oil prices following a report that US forces had struck an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz.

Investor fears about the vast sums being invested in the artificial intelligence complex have cast a pall over trading floors in the second half of the year, with many questioning firms’ profitability.

Earnings reports from titans including Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft have shown they will keep pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into data centres and chips even as investors grow impatient for returns.
Monday saw Apple post forecast-topping sales and profits but warned that its gross margin — the per centage of sales left after output costs — would drop in October-December.

Earlier, leading AI firm Anthropic posted a more than 1,100 per cent surge in quarterly revenue and nearly US$900 billion (RM3.67 trillion) in spending commitments as it counts down to its Wall Street listing later this month.
The investment pledges come amid a surge in borrowing costs, which have raised concerns about some companies’ financial positions owing to their huge debts, adding downward pressure to stock prices.
After a tough run last week, the selling continued at the start of this week with losses in Asian giants followed by their US counterparts on Wall Street where the Nasdaq ended 1.1 per cent off.
And there was not much improvement Tuesday — Seoul-listed SK hynix and Samsung tanked five per cent and 4.2 per cent respectively, dragging the Kospi down more than three per cent.
There were also losses in Taipei, Shanghai, Singapore, Manila, Bangkok and Jakarta, though Hong Kong, Sydney, Mumbai and Wellington edged up. Tokyo was closed for a holiday.
London, Frankfurt and Paris opened with losses.
Even a more than seven per cent plunge in oil prices Monday was unable to provide support.
The “collapse in crude should have been rocket fuel for the battered growth trade”, said SPI Asset Management’s Stephen Innes.
“Cheaper energy takes heat out of inflation, eases the rates pressure and normally gives long-duration tech a meaningful updraft.
“Instead, the Nasdaq handed back the entire opening bounce and broke Friday’s lows, a fairly ugly sign that the selling is now being driven by something deeper than oil, yields or the dollar.”
US President Donald Trump on Monday signalled progress in talks as Tehran said “intensive” exchanges were underway while offering to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions.
“But here’s the thing: we’re dealing from total strength. We can end it at any time. If I can make a deal, I’d rather do it, save a lot of lives.”

Vice President JD Vance separately said he and Trump were optimistic about securing an agreement, while Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian announced his government had been granted more authority by the supreme leader to pursue peace talks.
The country’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, added that “the ball is now in America’s court to prevent war”.

However, crude jumped more than one per cent Tuesday as the Wall Street Journal reported that US forces struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian state media reported five explosions in rapid succession.
The Journal added that they had not been publicly announced to avoid the impression Washington intended to resume major combat operations.
And National Australia Bank’s Rodrigo Catril offered a word of caution over the chances of peace.
“It is worth noting that the US and Iran’s positions have not materially changed,” he wrote in a commentary.

“Iran wants US restraint and economic relief (i.e. an end to hostilities, the lifting of the US naval blockade, relief from oil sanctions and the unfreezing of at least $12 billion in assets) before delivering the concessions Washington seeks, including the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.
“The US is demanding concessions related to Iran’s nuclear programme, but Iran wants to deal with the nuclear issue in separate talks at a later stage.
“Bottom line: for the stalemate to end, somebody needs to give ground, and it is unclear if either side is willing to do so.” — AFP
88eb9953ac71af8f: <!--kg-card-end: html--> A vibe-coded site that scraped Archive of Our Own (AO3) fanfiction works, reuploaded them and charged for audiobook versions is down now after the creator said they received over 2,000 takedown requests from authors in the single day it was up.

ao3.life, a website that sprung up following last week’s announced weeks-long outage of fanfiction repository AO3, scraped the internet for works to populate the site using “a swarm of AI Agents controlling 40 virtual machines were scraping the internet for all drives, scrapes, and sources,” the site’s creator, named Ganesh, wrote on a page apologizing for the entire project. AO3.life went down on Monday evening following widespread backlash from readers and authors on social media.
Before it went down, the ao3.life homepage said, “AO3, saved before it slips away. Search every fandom, ship and trope. Read it here, keep the EPUB, or let it read to you when your eyes get tired.”

AO3 went down on Thursday following a security incident, according to the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW) which owns the repository. The site is expected to be down for as long as four weeks. OTW says no data has been lost. Readers and authors are generally distraught, unable to access the site at all for potentially a month. AO3 hosts nearly 18.5 million works.

ao3.life offered works as EPUBs for reading on e-readers, and as AI-generated audiobooks that Ganesh charged for after the first three minutes. They claimed on a page titled “Authors get paid here” that authors would get 91% of the profits, with AO3.life getting 9% to cover “narration and processing” costs. “Your earnings wait for you. You don't need an account here to earn. We hold your share indefinitely until you collect it, however long that takes,” the site said.

On AO3, authors can “archive lock” their works, making them visible only to logged-in users, which keeps AI bots like this one from scraping them and also gives better control over how far a work spreads or whether it breaks the containment of the repository’s intended audience. Of course, authors couldn’t access AO3 while it was down to lock their works if they were publicly available before the outage.

But some authors reported the archive lock not mattering. “I had everything archive locked on ao3 and it's still all here and I as the author have 0 control over any of my fics on there,” one AO3 author posted on Bluesky.

ao3.life said at the bottom of the homepage that authors could request their works be removed from the site: ”Every work belongs to its author; if one is yours and you want it gone, email legal@ao3.life and it goes.” Proving that you’re the author of the work to ao3.life required authors “leave a note on your AO3 profile so we can confirm it's you,” the site said. But how authors could do that while AO3 was — and still is — completely down is a mystery.

A lot of authors clearly used the legal complaints email. “In the time this site has been up, I’ve facilitated over 2,000 takedown requests. It was never my intention to hurt so many authors - and I’m truly sorry to you all. There’s no way to show my sorry [sic] better than taking this site down,” Ganesh wrote. “Why did I charge for AI Slop audiobooks? I doubt anyone knows how expensive it is to run a server like this, especially with the amount of usage this site got. It had 126,592 unique users within 24 hours of going up, and had terabytes of bandwidth in usage. In an attempt to keep the site up, I thought audiobooks were a good option. I sold like 11 audiobooks, if it’s any consolation.”

Fanfiction has become a target of AI scraping, repackaging and reselling in recent years. In 2024, I reported on how Etsy sellers turn free fanfiction into printed and bound physical books, then list them for sale for as much as $100 a book.

With AO3 down and fans scrambling to find ways to keep consuming the works they miss, some people have started sharing links to Google Drives on Reddit and Discord of works they’d downloaded from the site previously, even if they aren’t the original authors of those works. This has alarmed and angered a lot of writers; whether authors have the right to profit from their works depends on the content and their use of existing intellectual property. Fanfic is typically considered fair use — I can write a VeggieTales Bob and Larry fic without getting sued by Universal Pictures if it’s sufficiently transformative, for example — but selling it could draw the ire of their lawyers, and a potential lawsuit even if I happened to ultimately win it. Authors on AO3 are prohibited by the platform from monetizing their works or linking to payment platforms.

“It was never and is not my intention to hurt authors, and I hope every subequent [sic] action I’ve taken is representative of that,” Ganesh said. “From an attempt at revenue sharing, to responding to takedown requests as fast as I could, to taking down the site as a whole.” They signed the note: “Yours truly, a 17 year old from India that thought they were doing something good.”
09d414a2d3db0b6a: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 3 — US chipmaking giant Nvidia is ordering its data centre partners to scale back work with Chinese customers, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.
Nvidia’s cloud computing clients must now sell at least 51 per cent of their services to non-Chinese companies, the FT reported, citing five people with knowledge of the matter.
The new rules only affect future contracts and not existing agreements, the report said.

Nvidia neither confirmed nor denied the report to AFP, but said in a statement that “datacentres and clouds built on American chips are the foundation that American model and application makers need to compete worldwide.”
“Longstanding US policy encourages every cloud to build on American infrastructure and to win business everywhere they can,” the statement said.
“America cannot win the AI race unless America’s AI infrastructure wins worldwide — if the world’s clouds rely on foreign-made chips, the model and application layers will be foreign-built as well.”
Asked about the report, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said she was not aware of it.

“As a matter of principle, we consistently hope that all parties can provide a fair, transparent and non-discriminatory business environment for companies from all countries, including Chinese companies,” she said.
China and the United States are locked in a race for dominance in the fast-moving artificial intelligence sector.
In recent months, the two countries have traded accusations of stealing AI technologies and jeopardising security.
Nvidia is the world’s most valuable company thanks to the global drive to build data centres packed with specialist computer chips and other hardware that runs AI systems. — AFP
8272e20d7aaa9a41: FRANKFURT, Nov 3 — German airline giant Lufthansa said Tuesday it expects its 2026 fuel costs to be €2 billion (RM9.12 billion) higher than last year as the Iran war keeps global energy prices elevated.
Releasing third quarter results, the group predicted its fuel bill across the full year will come in at €9.3 billion.
That is 600 million higher than it had anticipated just a few months ago, as the US war against Iran drags on.
The group, which also operates carriers including Swiss, Brussels and Eurowings, also slightly downgraded its forecast for core profit to a range of between €1.7 and €2.0 billion for 2026.
Previously it predicted a range of between €1.7 and €2.2 billion.
Despite the slightly bleaker outlook, the group reported a 30-per cent jump in profits for the July-September period, beating forecasts.
Net profit came in at €1.26 billion, with the company saying there had been strong demand for premium tickets to Asia and North America.
Revenues increased nine percent from a year earlier to €12.2 billion.
Fuel costs however were more than €500 million higher in the quarter compared to a year earlier.

“We improved our result compared with the previous year, despite higher fuel costs weighing on the quarterly result by more than half a billion euros — we are satisfied with that,” chief financial officer Till Streichert said.
“This was supported by robust demand in passenger traffic.” — AFP

But still Kemi Badenoch and the business lobby want to take us backwards Britain is unhappier at work than since records began. 76af35d96ed52712: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.

Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).

The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.

It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).

But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet.
So one month in, who’s on board?

Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a new request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period.

There have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon announced an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.

The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents).

As for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.
But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too.

In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.
But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.

Are Big Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated. The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia.
But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.

In an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently. But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway. Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.

Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too.

One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars. It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his company to implement that change. But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand. And, per the executive order, leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month.

But I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time and money. Surprisingly often I overhear strangers at a grocery store or coffee shop who have struck up a conversation about AI. The substance of the conversation is rarely uplifting—they most often talk about a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare—but what is heartening is how often I see a widespread desire among people to have a say in how this technology transforms their lives.

People may have wildly different feelings about AI, including outright hostility, but those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions that make it awkward for strangers to discuss immigration or climate change.

If “Super Intelligence” turns into a loyalty test, this will cease to be the case. It’s easy to imagine that two people chatting about, say, whether chatbots are good or bad for our mental health will stop once they realize one of them is saying “super intelligence” and the other “AI.” That would be a shame for us all.

Midterm elections are tomorrow. Americans say AI is more important to them in this election than environmental and climate policy (and Democrats even rank it above abortion and gun policy). We’re only just beginning to have a national conversation about what AI will mean for our lives. Whether or not “Super Intelligence” catches on, turning the terminology itself into a loyalty test will do nothing to advance a national conversation about AI that’s only just getting started.

4d54f679715f954d: Hong Kong ranks 24th in rule of law index and is trending down
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot from the World Justice Project's Rule of Law Index. Fair use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The Hong Kong anti-graft body, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), flaunted on X in early October that the city ranked in the top 10 globally and third in Asia in the “Absence of Corruption” category on the “Rule of Law Index 2026” published by the World Justice Project (WJP).

However, the “Absence of Corruption” merely captures whether or not public officials from the administration, police force, and judiciary use their offices for private gain; this single factor does not mean a society is free from corruption, as institutional favoritism, such as political nepotism, legal discrimination, and cronyism, are equally dangerous abuses of power that create systematic injustice. That’s why the WJP includes eight major factors in its index, and Hong Kong ranks 24th and scored 0.71 in the overall index among 143 countries, falling behind Australia (12), Singapore (14), Japan (15), and South Korea (20) in Asia and the Pacific. Between 2016 and 2020, Hong Kong consistently ranked 16th overall in the index.

The eight factors considered in the Rule of Law Index are “constraints on government power,” “absence of corruption,” “open government,” “fundamental rights,” “order and security,” “regulatory enforcement,” “civil justice,” and “criminal justice.”
Best performance: “order and security” and “absence of corruption”

Hong Kong performs best in “order and security” (ranked seventh with a 0.92 score), “absence of corruption” (ranked 10th with a 0.83 score), and “regulatory enforcement (ranked 16th with a 0.79 score). Among the subfactors of “order and security,” the city indeed has a relatively low crime rate (ranked eighth), and near-zero violent expression of grievance (ranked ninth).

In fact, the city has had hardly any protests since 2021, following the enactment of the National Security Law on June 30, 2020, and a heavy-handed crackdown on unauthorized protests. However, civic conflict remains high (ranked 40th), as people resort to street fights to express their frustrations.

The average Hongkonger will likely disagree with the relatively high ranking of “regulatory enforcement,” particularly after the recent release of the Taipo Deadly Fire investigation report, which revealed that multiple Hong Kong government authorities, including the Housing Bureau, the Labor Department, the Fire Service Department, and the Buildings Department, had not effectively enforced related regulations, which could have prevented the death of 168 individuals on November 25, 2025.

Moreover, while Hongkongers have complained about tender rigging in building renovations for over a decade, it was only after the high-profile Taipo fire that the authorities vowed to actively investigate the construction sector. Some fire victims also criticized the government’s buy-back plan as disrespectful of their private property rights. Both effectiveness of regulatory enforcement and respecting property rights are subfactors of “regulatory enforcement” in the Index.
Worst performance: “constraints in government's power” and “fundamental rights”
Hong Kong’s worst performance among the eight categories is “constraints in government’s power” (ranked 63rd with a 0.54 score) and “fundamental rights” (ranked 69th with a 0.55 score).

Hong Kong ranked 25th in “constraints in government’s power” in 2016, fell to 31st in 2020, then plummeted to 54th in 2022, and further tumbled to 63rd in 2025 and 2026. The enactment of the National Security Law in Hong Kong on June 30, 2020, which empowered the Hong Kong government to shut down independent media outlets and NGOs, was the main driving force in the recent plunges. Other factors included officials’ decision to rewrite electoral laws under the guiding principle of “patriots administering Hong Kong” in May 2021, the 2023 district council reform to restrict district councilors’ power and exclude oppositional figures, and the passage of domestic security law in March 2024 to outlaw acts including treason, espionage that harms the city, and incitement that provokes hatred. Rights groups say all of these provisions have chilled civil society activity and encroached on citizens’ fundamental rights.

The report described the “constraints in government’s power” performance as moderately to alarmingly risky, with constraints from the legislature ranking 84, judiciary 64, independent auditing and review bodies 61, non-government organizations 105, and the law 90 — the law refers to the legal framework that protects procedural justice and integrity regarding the appointment of officials and the electoral process. As for the subfactor “official sanctioned for misconduct,” which has a fair 22 ranking, some Hongkongers may consider the score too generous given that only one official has taken responsibility and resigned over the preventable Taipo Fire disaster.

A similar downward trend appears in the “fundamental rights” category, which ranked 29th in 2015, slipped to 38th in 2020, plummeted to 54th in 2021, and fell to 69th in 2026. The at-risk subfactors include security of suspects and dissidents (73), freedom of opinion and expression (105), privacy protection (86), freedom of assembly and association (115), and labor rights (66).

Hong Kong saw the shutdown of Apple Daily News and Stand News in 2021 upon the enactment of the National Security Law in 2020. The domestic Article 23 security law was enacted in March 2024 to further clamp down on “soft resistance” with the newly introduced sedition crime. Privacy rights have declined, as implementation rules for national security laws have empowered police to conduct physical searches of private property and digital devices without court warrants during national security investigations. Since 2020, NGOs, independent media outlets, and activist groups have vanished en masse amid a tightening political environment and shrinking civic space for organizational activities.
The fairly ranked subfactors are freedom from discrimination (29), rights of the accused and convicted (32), and freedom of religion (31).
Poor performance on “fundamental rights” also drags down the “open government” factor's rank (29), with its subfactor “civic participation” ranking 87 in an at-risk level.
Downgraded “civil justice” and “criminal justice”
Although Hong Kong's overall performance in civil and criminal justice remains fair, both factors have fallen from their historical high ranks of 11th and 7th to the current 20th and 23rd.
The main subfactors driving the decline in civil justice are discrimination (48) and improper government influence (56).

After the passage of Legal Aid Reforms in 2021, the number of applications to fund judicial review that challenge the government’s policy and decisions received by the Legal Aid Department dropped 60 percent from around 275 in 2016 to 110 in 2025. Of those 110 requests, the department approved only 2 cases. The overall number of judicial review cases fell from a peak of 3,899 in 2019 to 1,545 in 2022. Because most cases involve non-refoulement claims for refugee status, the government, in addition to the administrative Unified Screening Mechanism (USM) launched in 2014, introduced a special scheme in March 2025 to appoint eligible private practitioners as Deputy Judges of the Court of First Instance to handle these cases exclusively. The mechanism disposed of more than 3700 claims in 2025. Both reforms, driven by the government administration's political considerations, have negatively affected the poor and the non-citizen's access to judicial justice in Hong Kong.
The major subfactor contributing to the fall in criminal justice ranking is “government or political influence on the criminal justice system” (61).

Hong Kong’s criminal justice ranking first plunged in 2017, from 8th to 16th, after the government labeled the civil unrest in Mong Kok, dubbed the Fishball Revolution, as a riot and reactivated the colonial-era Public Order Ordinance to prosecute protesters en masse. Then, in 2021 and 2022, the ranking dropped again amid a series of speech-related national security prosecutions against 47 pro-democracy activists for participating in the primaries of the election of the legislature for conspiracy to subvert, Apple Daily senior executives for foreign collusion, and Stand News editors for conspiracy to publish seditious content. The recent convictions and heavy sentencing of Apple Daily’s executives, including Jimmy Lai, and former leaders over collusion, Albert Ho Chun-yan, Lee Chuek-yan and Chow Hang-tung, of the now-disbanded organizer of the June 4th candlelight vigil, Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, over inciting subversion, may further downgrade the city’s criminal justice performance in the next year. The fact that all these controversial cases were handled by judges designated by the Chief Executive adds weight to the evaluation of “government or political influence on the criminal justice system”.

According to the Index’s insights, the global rule of law has declined for 9 consecutive years. Civic participation and the freedoms of speech and assembly each fell in over 60 percent of countries, and Hong Kong is among them. The city also sees the global trend of improper government influence that undermines civil and criminal justice.

The Rule of Law Index is particularly crucial to global financial centers; as the WJP notes, when the index scores reach 0.66, countries tend to have high sovereign credit ratings. Currently, Hong Kong’s score is 0.71 and trending down, while its Asian competitor, Singapore, ranks 14th with a 0.79 score and an upward trend. Watchdogs indicate this could be a bad sign for the city as it seeks to secure its spot as the region’s top economy.
Written by Oiwan Lam
c064ec7bcbb77124: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source, after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.
The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].
The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”
Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”
“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

9de50d9e2df39599: Baru-baru ini calon muda Pakatan Harapan (PH) bagi kerusi Kuala Linggi pada PRN Melaka, menarik perhatian ramai apabila mendakwa berjaya membantu menyelesaikan masalah penalti cukai lebih RM70,000 yang menghimpit sebuah persatuan nelayan sejak beberapa tahun lalu. Kemudian calon tersebut mengisytiharkan ‘This is how Gen Z works (beginilah cara Gen Z bekerja)’.

Kenyataan itu mengundang pelbagai reaksi. Penyokong parti menyatakan inilah generasi yang kita mahu, muda dan pantas tidak seperti pemimpin tua yang lambat, malas dan banyak main politik. Penyokong parti lawan pula sudah pastilah mentertawakan dan memperlekehkan kenyataan tersebut. Katanya 'budak ini' berangan.

Dakwaan calon tersebut menggambarkan seolah-olah selama ini orang tua tidak mampu menjadi pelaksana yang berkesan. Memang di media sosial pun sering kita lihat warga Malaysia bawah 60 tahun menyatakan rasa muaknya melihat muka pak cik-pak cik di Parlimen yang telah pun mereka lihat sejak kecil lagi. Sebab itu selalu timbul saranan agar kita tolak pemimpin tua dalam pilihan raya.

Soalannya, apakah sekarang kita benar-benar perlukan orang muda sebagai peneraju barisan hadapan dalam pentadbiran negara? Dan kali ini calon Gen Z sendiri telah mengangkat dirinya dan mendakwa generasinya mampu mengambil alih kerja ini dengan lebih efisien.

Di Threads sering saya lihat Gen Z bertekak dengan Gen Y (milenial). Masing-masing mahu membuktikan generasi merekalah paling bagus. Maksudnya, kami Gen X dan Boomers ni kira dinosaurlah, kena duduk di tepi diam-diam.

Tapi benar, memang perkembangan dunia hari ini sedang menyaksikan kebangkitan politik anak muda. Di Nepal, demonstrasi besar-besaran pada September 2025 yang digerakkan anak muda akibat kemarahan terhadap rasuah, nepotisme dan sekatan media sosial akhirnya membawa kepada kejatuhan kerajaan. Pada Mac 2026, Balendra Shah, bekas penyanyi rap berusia 35 tahun muncul sebagai perdana menteri baharu negara itu. Walaupun Shah sendiri tergolong dalam Gen Y, naiknya dia sebagai perdana menteri tidak dapat dipisahkan daripada gelombang perubahan yang digerakkan oleh Gen Z.

Di Kenya, anak muda bangkit menentang dasar percukaian dan tekanan ekonomi. Di Madagascar, anak muda bangkit melawan kerajaan. Di Maghribi menyaksikan gerakan bernama 'Gen Z 212' mendesak kerajaan melakukan pembaharuan pendidikan dan perkhidmatan kesihatan. Seperti kesan domino, walaupun tiada kaitan di antara mereka, kebangkitan anak muda ini semakin melebar ke serata dunia.

Paling baru bulan lepas dan masih berlaku, anak muda Perancis bangkit memprotes besar-besaran isu pendidikan sehingga memberikan tekanan kepada Presiden Emmanuel Macron. Gelombang rakyat kemudiannya menjadi makin besar dan merebak sehingga menarik penyertaan mahasiswa, kesatuan sekerja dan masyarakat umum memprotes isu-isu lain juga.

Ini memperlihatkan satu fenomena di mana golongan yang selama ini sering dianggap lembik dan cepat layu seperti strawberi tiba-tiba mampu mengucar-ngacirkan kestabilan politik sebuah negara. Apakah Malaysia juga sedang bergerak ke arah itu? Nampaknya calon Kuala Linggi ini cuba membayangkan bahawa proses pengambilalihan anak muda boleh bermula.

Melihat perkembangan dunia, kita tahu protes anak muda di jalan raya bukan perkara baru tetapi perlu ditegaskan bahawa menjatuhkan kerajaan dengan mentadbir kerajaan merupakan dua perkara berbeza. Semua orang boleh marah dan turun memprotes menumbangkan kerajaan. Semua orang boleh berceramah tetapi bukan semua boleh merangka dasar, merancang belanjawan dan mengurus ekonomi. Yang dulu kaki demo, kini sudah jadi menteri pun kita dapat lihat dia masih terpinga-pinga. Yang dah berhenti jadi menteri pun kita lihat banyak bercakap di podcast komplen sana-sini walhal sewaktu jadi menteri entah apa yang dia buat, tak nampak pun hasilnya.

Sebenarnya, kemunculan pemimpin muda bukan perkara baharu dalam sejarah politik negara kita. Najib Razak menjadi Ahli Parlimen ketika berusia 23 tahun, dilantik sebagai timbalan menteri pada usia 25 tahun dan menjadi menteri besar Pahang ketika berusia 29 tahun.

'Pengantin baru' Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman pun pernah menjadi menteri belia dan sukan pada usia 25 tahun. Kini, di kementerian sama menyaksikan Mohammed Taufiq Johari, menjawat jawatan menteri dalam usia tak sampai 30 tahun. Maknanya, kebolehan orang muda memimpin memang sentiasa diiktiraf. Bezanya dulu kita tidak melabelkan seseorang mengikut generasi yang bunyinya macam bunyi model telefon pintar atau kereta. Gen itulah, gen inilah!

Sebenarnya, saya sendiri rimas dengan label dan pembahagian kategori manusia kepada Baby Boomers, Gen X, Gen Y, Gen Z, Alpha dan bermacam-macam generasi lagi. Bagi saya, label tersebut bukanlah ketetapan saintifik yang mutlak. Label generasi yang pada asalnya digunakan dalam kajian sosial ini kemudian telah menjadi alat pemasaran dalam dunia perniagaan.

Dalam dunia pemasaran, pengguna perlu dikenal pasti, dikelompokkan supaya produk dapat dijual dengan lebih berkesan. Meletakkan label pada generasi adalah satu jalan mudah untuk tujuan tersebut. Masalah yang timbul ialah apabila kategori pemasaran ini mula dianggap sebagai kebenaran fakta tentang sifat manusia. Boomers beginilah, Gen X begitulah, kononnya mereka lebih lasak tapi menjadi hamba pekerjaan. Generasi sekarang pula lebih pintarlah, tetapi lembik macam strawberi. Macam saya kata tadi, kebenaran teori itu tidak mutlak dan bergantung kepada banyak faktor.

Padahal, perbezaan yang diperdebatkan selalu ini hanya sekadar pertembungan biasa antara golongan tua dengan orang muda. Orang muda dulu pun memberontak dan mempertikaikan kewibawaan orang tua yang dirasakan sudah mula tumpul. Kita waktu muda dahulu pun rebel, mahu bebas dan bercita-cita mengubah dunia. Manakala orang tua adatnya pula sentiasa meragui keupayaan anak muda. Macam kita hari ini berat untuk menyerahkan baton kerana menganggap anak muda masih belum cukup matang dan kurang pengalaman.

Di Malaysia pula, budaya politiknya memang sudah 'begitu' sejak sekian lama. Anak muda yang mahu menjadi pemimpin kebanyakannya masih perlu melalui struktur parti yang dikuasai generasi tua. Mereka perlu mendapat restu kepimpinan, mematuhi disiplin parti dan menyesuaikan diri dengan budaya politik sedia ada ini. Pendek kata, dengan acuan politik tua, Gen Z yang berada di dalamnya pun akan kelihatan poyo dan tak menarik. Itulah yang berlaku ketika Baby Boomers, Gen X dan milenial masih muda. Mahu mengubah, bercakap lantang tentang kebangkitan anak muda tetapi akhirnya tersedut ke dalam lubang yang sama.

Apakah boleh terjadi satu gelombang di mana anak muda Gen Z beramai-ramai menyertai mana-mana parti politik besar tanah air dan melakukan 'serang hendap' mengambil alih tampuk kepimpinan lama lalu melakukan reformasi politik? Sempatkah mereka naik atau belum apa-apa mereka semua akan dicantas?

Kepada calon Kuala Linggi, saya mengalu-alukan calon muda tetapi saya kira keberkesanan seseorang pemimpin bukan diukur dengan cepat atau lambatnya mendapat tandatangan perdana menteri. Itu masih belum dianggap satu perubahan. Dan kalau itulah yang dikatakan sebagai satu kerja, ia bukanlah sesuatu yang membanggakan. Budaya surat sokongan, budaya potong barisan guna kabel politik bukan perkara baru dan bukan budaya yang sihat.

Jika Gen Z bercita-cita untuk melakukan reformasi, ia harus mempercekapkan sistem pentadbiran itu sendiri tanpa banyak kerenah birokrasi dalam menyelesaikan masalah rakyat. Jika itu berjaya, kita tak perlukan hubungan istimewa wakil rakyat dengan Perdana Menteri untuk meluluskan sebarang pekerjaan. Kita mahu kecekapan sistem itu sendiri yang memainkan peranan dengan berkesan. Itu yang harus anak muda Gen Z ubah jika berjaya menjadi perangka dasar di Dewan Rakyat.

Persoalan sama ada Gen Z mampu memimpin negara tidak boleh dijawab dengan melihat kad pengenalan, kepetahan berpidato, jumlah 'follower' TikTok atau aktif menghasilkan video. Kita memerlukan pemimpin yang memahami tanggungjawab, mempunyai keberanian membuat keputusan, menghormati institusi dan sanggup dipertanggungjawabkan apabila melakukan kesilapan. Ciri-ciri tersebut tetap ada pada sesetengah pemimpin tua kita hari ini. Sekiranya ada ahli politik dari Gen Z yang tidak memenuhi kriteria tersebut, pada saya dia hanyalah mesin baharu dengan program lama.

Sesebuah negara itu hebat kerana pemimpinnya sentiasa mempunyai idea segar, bertenaga dan bersemangat melaksanakan visinya tanpa mengira berapa pun usianya. Tetapi jika pemimpin generasi muda terus membawa perangai politik lama yang poyo dan main -main, nescaya kita tidak akan ke mana-mana. Harap muka sahaja muda, idea dan wawasannya tetap lapuk. 12205f0e791d641a: It will cut the bureacratic red tape that plagues state institutions
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Sbunker. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

One of the biggest barriers for people’s effective engagement with the authorities in Kosovo is a confusing and unresponsive bureaucracy. Whenever citizens want to report a problem in their community, such as potholes or illegal waste disposal, they are met with a system that requires them to know the roles and responsibilities of various state institutions and handle necessary paperwork themselves.

When submitted to the wrong agency or without proper documents, citizens’ complaints are either ignored or can take long periods to be processed, which discourages engagement and has an adverse effect on people’s trust in the government. Ultimately, it deteriorates the already challenging situation regarding transparency, communication, and accountability of state bodies in Kosovo.

In 2026, a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Sbunker, responded to this challenge by creating an online platform called Kosovo.report to help citizens report their complaints to the authorities in a quick and easy manner. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Hana Deva, project manager at SBunker, to learn more about their initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Hana Deva (HD): Sbunker is a non-governmental organization founded in 2016, focused on providing analysis and informed perspectives on important political, economic, social, and cultural issues in Kosovo and the Western Balkans.

Through our Disinfo program, we monitor local and regional media content to identify and address disinformation. Sbunker produces podcasts and other media content exploring political and social developments, philosophical, cultural, and theoretical discussions.

We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to create a direct form of civic engagement through technology. This led to the development of Kosovo.report, a platform designed to give citizens a simple way to report problems and submit requests concerning their neighborhoods and local communities.
The platform is intended to act as a link between citizens and public institutions by helping these reports reach the relevant institutions and making the process more accessible to the citizens.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
HD: Through our work in media and civic engagement, we became interested in how citizens communicate everyday problems in their communities to public institutions.

Research on public administration in Kosovo points to fragmented public service delivery, inconsistencies in administrative procedures and digital services, and continuing challenges in communication between citizens and institutions.
This can make the process of reporting an issue to the right department unclear.

Kosovo.report was developed with this challenge in mind. The idea is to give citizens a more straightforward way to report an issue, without requiring them to first determine which institution or department is responsible.
Based on the type and location of the problem, the platform is designed to route the report to the appropriate department and allow the citizen to follow what happens afterwards.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
HD: Our main work has been the development of Kosovo.report, from the initial concept to a functional platform now being prepared for its pilot phase.

Alongside this development, we have coordinated with the Municipality of Prishtina to determine how reports should reach the appropriate departments, and prepared a Memorandum of Understanding to formalise this cooperation.

Beyond the platform, Sbunker has served as a capacity hub for other Digital Sparks project grantees during the project period. We organized meetings and an advocacy workshop where grantees worked on developing a joint advocacy event.

We also hosted a young fellow, Bora Dibra, from the Albanian organization IRSH (Young Intellectuals, Hope), for a one-month fellowship focused on digital civic engagement, media literacy, and participatory advocacy.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.
HD: The project has allowed Sbunker to expand the way we approach civic engagement. Much of our work traditionally focused on informing citizens and creating public debate through publications.

Through Kosovo.report, we are developing a tool that takes this a step further by giving citizens a channel through which they can raise problems in their communities and have their reports directed to the relevant departments.
The next step will be the pilot of Kosovo.report in the capital, Prishtina, where we will be able to test the platform with citizens, gather their feedback, and identify what needs to be improved.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?
HD: Developing Kosovo.report has given us experience in creating a digital tool through which citizens can report issues and direct them to the relevant departments.

The process has also involved working with the Municipality of Prishtina as we prepare for the pilot phase of the project, which is a different scope of work from Sbunker's focus on media and public debate.

Our role as a capacity hub has also given us an opportunity to work more closely with individual grantees and other civil society organizations, learn about their projects in digital democracy, and the challenges in their communities.

Taken together, these activities have expanded Sbunker’s experience from media, analysis and public debate, to developing digital tools and working more closely with civil society organizations and public institutions.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

HD: One of the most valuable experiences has been developing something that is intended to have a direct use in people’s everyday lives. With Kosovo.report, we are taking a different approach by developing a platform that citizens can use in their communities and communicate with relevant institutions.
Building the platform has also given us a better sense of what it takes to turn an idea for civic participation into something that works in practice.
The capacity hub and fellowship have added to this experience by allowing us to work with people approaching digital democracy and civic engagement from different projects and contexts.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

HD: For us, Kosovo.report is a starting point for what we want to do in the digital democracy area. The current focus is on Prishtina, but we want to take the platform beyond the pilot and explore opportunities to connect with other municipalities and public institutions across Kosovo.
The first phase is helping us see what works, what needs to be improved, and how the platform can better respond to the needs of local communities.

The project has also strengthened Sbunker’s capacity to develop digital approaches to civic participation. We want to build on that experience in our future work by looking more closely at the needs of the communities we work with and explore where digital tools can help address them.
We also want to continue the relationships developed through this project, both with civil society organizations and collaborators, and see where they can lead beyond the project.

1a7942fb3b9f842f: Diplomacy is not always measured by grand agreements, historic handshakes or comprehensive peace settlements.
Sometimes, its effectiveness is demonstrated through small but tangible improvements in human lives.
The recent decision by Myanmar’s military authorities to begin releasing ethnic Rakhine deportees following Malaysian diplomatic pressure is one such development.
According to The Irrawaddy, the releases followed Malaysia’s intervention over the detention of individuals deported from Malaysia to Myanmar.
This is hardly a diplomatic breakthrough. Yet it is not insignificant.
It demonstrates that Putrajaya’s decision to maintain engagement with Nay Pyi Taw, despite international criticism, can produce limited but measurable results.
More baby steps are needed.
First, engagement must never be confused with endorsement.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has faced criticism for engaging Myanmar’s military leadership, particularly Senior General now President Min Aung Hlaing.
Critics argue that such engagement risks legitimising a regime responsible for widespread displacement, military violence and the destruction of democratic institutions.
These concerns are valid.

However, refusing to communicate with the authorities exercising power in Nay Pyi Taw would make it harder for Malaysia to secure detainees’ release, negotiate humanitarian access or protect vulnerable returnees.
Diplomacy requires contact, even with governments whose conduct one fundamentally opposes.
The purpose is not to confer legitimacy but to influence behaviour.
Second, the releases demonstrate the potential value of sustained diplomatic pressure.
Malaysia raised concerns about the treatment of its deportees. Foreign minister Mohamad Hasan sought clarification. Myanmar subsequently began releasing those detained.
Although this sequence does not prove that Malaysian pressure alone led to the releases, it suggests that diplomatic intervention mattered.
Malaysia did not merely accept Myanmar’s treatment of the deportees. It demanded accountability.
This is how engagement should function: dialogue accompanied by expectations, verification and humanitarian safeguards.
Third, piecemeal progress must not conceal Myanmar’s larger humanitarian catastrophe.
Without a doubt, Myanmar remains deeply fractured.
The military authorities do not exercise uncontested control over the entire country.
Ethnic armed organisations and resistance forces remain powerful actors.
Rakhine State is particularly complicated because of the continuing conflict involving the Arakan Army and Myanmar’s military.
Repatriation cannot automatically be considered safe merely because some detainees have been released.
Malaysia must distinguish between voluntary returns and deportations that expose vulnerable people to persecution, detention or forced recruitment.
The principle of non-refoulement must remain central.
Fourth, Malaysia needs stronger mechanisms to monitor returnees.
Diplomatic assurances are meaningful only when independently verified.
Malaysia should work with relevant UN agencies and humanitarian organisations to establish procedures for monitoring the welfare of those returned.
Such arrangements should protect family contact, freedom from arbitrary detention and access to humanitarian assistance.
Without verification, Malaysia risks celebrating releases without knowing whether those individuals subsequently enjoy meaningful security.
Fifth, Asean must translate Malaysia’s incremental progress into collective diplomatic action.
To be sure, the Asean Five-Point Consensus has struggled to end Myanmar’s conflict.
Nevertheless, its fundamental objectives remain relevant: reducing violence, encouraging inclusive dialogue and facilitating humanitarian assistance.
Malaysia’s bilateral engagement should complement these objectives, not replace them.
The Philippines, as Asean Chair in 2026, should consider how such diplomatic openings can strengthen regional cooperation.
Asean needs more than repeated expressions of concern.
It needs Asean’s resolve to translate principles into practical humanitarian outcomes.
Sixth, engagement must extend beyond Myanmar’s military leadership.
Malaysia should maintain communication with the National Unity Government (the Myanmar government-in-exile), ethnic armed organisations, civil society and humanitarian networks.
Myanmar’s fragmentation makes broader engagement indispensable.
A settlement negotiated exclusively with military authorities cannot guarantee acceptance throughout the country.
Malaysia must broaden and deepen its diplomatic channels without abandoning humanitarian principles.
Finally, Anwar’s approach should be judged by outcomes rather than appearances.
Malaysia cannot single-handedly resolve Myanmar’s civil war.
But neither should it abandon opportunities to secure modest improvements in human security.
The release of Rakhine deportees is encouraging, although it does not establish that Myanmar has fundamentally changed.
Further progress requires humanitarian access, independent monitoring, safeguards for returnees and eventually inclusive political dialogue.
Myanmar’s crisis cannot be resolved overnight. Yet diplomatic paralysis is not a strategy.
Malaysia must remain principled without becoming immobilised by the complexity of Myanmar’s conflict.
The journey towards peace may begin with small humanitarian concessions rather than spectacular diplomatic breakthroughs.
More baby steps are needed. But genuine, verifiable and sustainable piecemeal progress is still progress.
For Myanmar’s long-suffering people, even modest improvements in human security matter.

de929831445c05d5: Walaupun seminggu sudah berlalu saya terpanggil menulis mengenai Perjanjian Keyakinan dan Perbekalan dimeterai antara kerajaan, Ahli Parlimen Bersatu, bekas Ahli Parlimen parti itu yang menyokong PMX dan Ahli Parlimen Muar Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.

Sebab? Perikatan Nasional memutuskan tidak akan ikut sama yakni tidak akan menandatangani perjanjian itu yang ramai lebih gemar guna istilah Inggerisnya iaitu CSA untuk Confidence and Supply Agreement.

PN jelas tidak bersependapat lalu tidak menerima CSA. Itu hak mereka. Cuma yang menarik bagi saya ialah rakan baik PN (khususnya dalam menghadapi PRN Melaka) iaitu Pengerusi BN Zahid Hamidi menyarankan CSA diperluas kepada lebih banyak parti sama ada daripada kerajaan atau pembangkang.

Sebab kedua ialah apabila Zahid berkata (saya ulang ) “apa yang dilakukan ini (CSA) satu langkah baik dan pernah dilaksanakan kerajaan ketika wakil Umno jadi perdana menteri”.

Wakil Ummo jadi perdana menteri yang dimaksudkan kita tahu ialah Ismail Sabri Yaakob. Apa yang berlaku? Tentu ramai masih ingat. Pada September 2021, Ismail memeterai apa yang dipanggil memorandum persefahaman dan kestabilan politik dengan Anwar Ibrahim yang waktu itu ketua pembangkang.
Kata Anwar, memorandum itu menjadi kenyataan kerana sikap positif Ismail yang mengambil pendekatan berunding segera dengan pembangkang sebaik dilantik perdana menteri kesembilan.

Perlu dinyatakan memorandum itu bukan CSA per se. Ini diakui Anwar sendiri waktu itu. Apa pun dalam dokumen MoU antara Pakatan Harapan dengan kerajaan pimpinan Ismail, kerajaan menjanjikan sejumlah reformasi dalam jangka waktu tertentu dan juga berjanji untuk tidak membubarkan Parlimen sebelum 31 Julai 2022.

Sebagai balasan PH pula berjanji tidak akan menggunakan undi mereka menggulingkan Ismail atau menyekat Belanjawan 2022 selagi pembaharuan dijanjikan mengikut jadual dan pembangkang dilibatkan dalam perbincangan Rang Undang-undang Perbekalan. Namun, Zahid dan Umno menekan Ismail untuk mengadakan pilihan raya umum dengan segera kerana berpendapat Umno sedang berada pada tahap meyakinkan untuk menang. Zahid konon mahu Ismail strike while the iron is still hot.
Tindakan Zahid dan Umno boleh dilihat sebagai tidak memberi ruang kepada Ismail menjayakan MoU beliau dengan PH.

Tekanan demi tekanan dikenakan ke atas Ismail. Menyulitkan Ismail ialah beliau sekadar seorang naib presiden Umno manakala Zahid presiden parti . Akhirnya, Ismail tidak ada pilihan melainkan tunduk akur. Parlimen dibubarkan pada Oktober 2022 dan PRU15 diadakan pada November 2022.
Dan Umno/BN mencatat prestasi paling buruk dalam sejarah mereka. Umno hanya menang 27 kerusi, MCA (2) dan MIC (1). Perkiraan Zahid meleset.

Fast forward CSA yang dimeterai 29 Okt lalu. Pada upacara tandatangan kerajaan diketuai Timbalan Perdana Menteri II Fadillah Yusof. Bukan timbalan perdana menteri I. Kita tahu siapa pemegang jawatan itu.
Mungkinkah ini kerana pendirian lalu Zahid terhadap MoU 2021 dan tindakan susulannya yang boleh dilihat sebagai bertentangan dengan semangat MoU itu?
Maka, kerana itulah saya tersenyum lebar seperti disebut tadi apabila Zahid memuji CSA 2026 dan mahu ia diperluas kepada semua parti.
